one_liner: Research double-precision BLAS for AVX-512 Intel CPUs with built-in soft-error checks; paper reports small wins over OpenBLAS, BLIS, MKL.
what_it_does: FT-BLAS is the code behind an ICS '21 paper: hand-written x86 kernels for a subset of BLAS (mostly double precision: level-1 dasum/daxpy/ddot/dnrm2/drot/dscal etc., level-2 dgemv/dger/dtrsv/dsyr/banded and packed routines, level-3 dgemm/dsymm/dtrmm/dtrsm, plus a few single-precision level-1 routines). It exposes CBLAS-named functions (cblas_dgemm, cblas_ddot, ...) through its own cblas.h, and a CMake switch -DUSE_FAULT_TOLERANT=ON swaps every wrapper to a fault-tolerant variant at build time. There is no runtime choice and no LAPACK.
how_it_is_fast: The non-FT kernels are Goto-style blocked GEMM (A/B packing into 4 KiB-aligned buffers, KC=384, 24x8 AVX-512 micro-kernel in inline assembly with software prefetch) and unrolled AVX2/AVX-512 assembly loops for level-1/2. For fault tolerance, the paper uses a hybrid scheme: dual modular redundancy (each FMA issued twice into separate registers and compared with vpcmpeqd/vmovmskpd) for memory-bound level-1/2, where the duplicate instructions hide behind memory stalls, and algorithm-based fault tolerance (row/column checksums of A, B and C) for level-3, with the checksum updates fused into the packing routines so they cost almost no extra memory traffic.
when_to_use: Research or evaluation of soft-error-tolerant linear algebra on Intel Skylake-SP / Cascade Lake class CPUs with AVX-512.
Studying or borrowing a compact, readable AVX-512 DGEMM (Goto blocking + 24x8 assembly micro-kernel) or DMR-in-assembly level-1 kernels as a starting point for your own code, under GPL-3.0 terms.
Single-node, double-precision, column-major, non-transposed GEMM/DOT/AXPY workloads where you can test that your exact call shapes are supported.
when_not_to_use: As a production replacement for OpenBLAS, MKL or BLIS: many argument combinations are unimplemented (cblas_dgemm accepts only ColMajor NoTrans/NoTrans; dsymm only Left/Lower; dtrsm and dtrmm only Left/Lower/NoTrans) and the library calls exit(-1) on anything else.

Code that relies on alpha == 0 semantics: the dgemm, dsymm, dtrmm and dtrsm wrappers return immediately when alpha is 0, leaving C unscaled by beta (or B not zeroed), which violates the BLAS specification.

Anyone who needs the fault tolerance to actually protect results: in the released DGEMM the checksum comparison and correction code is commented out, and the fault-tolerant DDOT on a detected mismatch only prints a message and returns a truncated (wrong) dot product instead of recomputing.
Non-AVX-512 CPUs, AMD/ARM machines, complex or most single-precision routines, or multithreaded BLAS: CMake hard-codes -march=skylake-avx512 and the DGEMM/DDOT sources contain no threading.
Closed-source or permissively licensed products: the code is GPL-3.0.

integration.form: static lib (CMake add_library without SHARED; builds libSrcFuncs plus test binaries)
integration.dependencies: none beyond libm and libpthread; CMake passes -fopenmp
integration.min_toolchain: C++11, CMake 3.17; GCC/Clang-style inline assembly (AT&T syntax) and AVX-512 intrinsics; the paper used icc 19.0 -O3
integration.platforms: x86-64 Linux with AVX-512F (Skylake-SP, Cascade Lake or newer Intel); -march=skylake-avx512 is hard-coded
integration.thread_safety: not documented; DGEMM allocates its packing buffers per call with aligned_alloc and uses no globals in the code read, but no statement exists
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — exports CBLAS names and enums for the supported subset, so simple ColMajor double-precision code can relink against it, but unsupported cases abort the process, alpha==0 handling is wrong, several output pointers are declared const, and its cblas.h clashes with OpenBLAS/MKL headers

gotchas: Unsupported layout/transpose/side combinations and bad leading dimensions call printf then exit(-1) or exit(-2) from inside the library instead of returning an error code.
Each DGEMM call allocates about 32 MB of packing buffers (384x1152 and 384x9216 doubles) and frees them on return, which hurts repeated small calls.
The fault-tolerant DGEMM compares checksums against an absolute threshold of 1e-2 (in commented-out code), which would false-alarm on large-magnitude data and miss small errors if re-enabled.
The top-level CMake overwrites CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS with CMAKE_C_FLAGS plus its own flags, so CXX flags passed by the user are dropped.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick FT-BLAS only when soft-error tolerance on x86 is the research question, since no catalogued sibling offers it; for plain speed on CPUs, BLASFEO or LibShalom (small matrices) and GEMMFIP or Eigen (general sizes) are complete, maintained and permissively licensed, and CLBlast is the GPU option.
verified_claims_summary: The peer-reviewed ICS '21 paper reports FT-BLAS (including its fault-tolerant variants) up to 22.14% faster than OpenBLAS, 21.70% faster than BLIS and 3.50% faster than Intel MKL across routines from all three BLAS levels, built with icc 19.0 -O3 on an Intel Xeon Gold 5122 (Skylake) and a Xeon W-2255 (Cascade Lake), with fault-tolerance overhead under 3% while errors were injected. These are best-case 'up to' figures, and the repository's test programs time only FT-BLAS itself, so the comparison is not reproducible from the repo.
status_note: Abandoned research code (last commit 2023-02-28, 7 stars, no releases); GPL-3.0 with an OpenBLAS license file included, usable for study or experiments but not production-ready.
